name: Lead Belly's grave, Shiloh Baptist Church
writeup: Huddie Ledbetter, known as Lead Belly, was born around 1885 on the Jeter Plantation near Mooringsport and died on December 6, 1949. He is buried in the cemetery behind Shiloh Baptist Church, outside the town, under a dark granite stone engraved with his twelve-string guitar. He carried field hollers, ballads and blues such as "Goodnight Irene" and "The Midnight Special" from Caddo Parish to a national audience after the folklorist John Lomax met him in 1933 and recorded him for the Library of Congress. The grave lies in the same parish where that journey began.

name: Stan's Record Shop and Jewel, Paula and Ronn Records (site)
writeup: In 1948 Stan Lewis bought a tiny record shop at 728 Texas Street and put his own name on it. Over roughly the next 37 years it grew into six stores, a nationwide mail-order and distribution business, and three labels: Jewel (1963), Paula (1965) and Ronn (1967). Lewis passed Dale Hawkins's "Susie Q" to Chess's Checker label, which released it in 1957, and Paula had his biggest hit with "Judy in Disguise" by John Fred and His Playboy Band. Jewel leaned toward blues and gospel, Ronn toward R&B. The building is gone, and a parking lot occupies the spot.

name: Jimmie Davis Tabernacle
writeup: Friends of Governor Jimmie Davis built this tabernacle in 1964 on the grounds in the Beech Springs community where he finished high school and where his parents' house once stood. Davis, born here in Jackson Parish in 1899, was a country recording star before he was governor, and his "You Are My Sunshine" became a state song; from the 1950s he recorded a great deal of gospel. The marker says the builders were devoted to "the songs of Christian inspiration," and the building serves as a gospel meeting hall. Davis died in 2000 at 101 and is buried in the cemetery at the tabernacle.

name: Rebel State Historic Site and Louisiana Country Music Museum
writeup: The site began with a grave. In 1962 local people put up a marker over an unknown Confederate soldier buried in these woods and started holding yearly ceremonies, and over the years the gatherings made the place a destination for country and gospel musicians and their fans. The state now runs it as a historic site with an amphitheater for bluegrass, country, gospel and folk concerts and the Louisiana Country Music Museum. Its exhibits follow the region's music from early gospel and string bands to modern country, give two rooms to the Louisiana Hayride, and include a fiddle that belonged to Roy Acuff.

name: Original True Light Baptist Church (Winnsboro Easter Rock)
writeup: On the night before Easter, women in white carry oil lamps counterclockwise around a table that stands for Christ's tomb, singing call-and-response spirituals over the beat of their own feet on the wooden floor. This is the Easter Rock, a ritual that Black Baptist congregations in the northeast Louisiana Delta have kept since before the Civil War and that scholars connect to the ring shout. It once ranged from East Carroll to Concordia Parish; the Winnsboro group, led by Hattie Addison Burkhalter, is the only one known to continue. Burkhalter, born in 1953, first took part at age six. The ensemble received a National Heritage Fellowship in 2021.

name: Grambling State University Tiger Marching Band (Conrad Hutchinson Jr. Performing Arts Center)
writeup: Grambling's band began in 1926, when Ralph Waldo Emerson Jones, later the school's longtime president, obtained seventeen instruments from Sears and Roebuck. Conrad Hutchinson Jr. arrived as director in 1952 and over 39 years built the group into the "World Famed" Tiger Marching Band. It played halftime at the first Super Bowl in 1967, the inauguration of Liberia's president in 1972, and Super Bowl IX in New Orleans in 1975, and appeared in a Coca-Cola television commercial in 1981. The campus performing arts center carries Hutchinson's name. Today the band marches 250 to 300 members, most of them from out of state.

name: Isaac Greggs Band Hall, Southern University (Human Jukebox)
writeup: Southern University's marching band was established in 1947 by T. Leroy Davis, who directed it until 1964. Isaac Greggs took over in 1969 and gave it the name Human Jukebox, because the band could play the top 40 hits of the day. Under Greggs it spent weeks at Radio City Music Hall in 1972, giving 140 performances, first played the Bayou Classic at the Louisiana Superdome in 1975, and appeared at Super Bowls, Sugar Bowls and presidential inaugurations. In 2003 the university's music building, on the campus in north Baton Rouge, was renamed the Isaac Greggs Band Hall in his honor.

name: Teddy's Juke Joint
writeup: Lloyd "Teddy" Johnson Jr. was born in 1946 in this small shotgun house off Old Scenic Highway, on property his grandmother bought around 1920. In 1979 he opened it as a juke joint, and he has run it ever since, spinning blues records himself between live shows by local, regional and national players. Christmas lights stay up all year, and his childhood tricycle hangs from the ceiling. Few places of the kind survive, and the Blues Foundation gave Johnson its Keeping the Blues Alive Award in 2023. The house stands along Highway 61 north of Baton Rouge.

name: Abita Springs Opry (Abita Springs Town Hall)
writeup: Six times a year the old wooden town hall in Abita Springs fills for the Abita Springs Opry, a concert series run by a nonprofit to preserve and present Louisiana roots music, played mostly acoustically. Since 2002 its programs have centered on old-time country, bluegrass and traditional Southern gospel, with Cajun, zydeco, Irish and traditional New Orleans jazz bands sharing the bill. The series has had a single cancellation, after Hurricane Katrina, and reached its hundredth show in 2019. The hall is more than a hundred years old, with pecky cypress walls, wooden floors and room for just under four hundred listeners.

name: Twin City Jamboree (Ouachita Valley Fairgrounds site)
writeup: From 1953 to 1970 the Twin City Jamboree drew Saturday-night crowds to the old Ouachita Valley Fairgrounds in West Monroe for a home-grown country and bluegrass stage show. Local partners including Alex Myatt and Jack Hollingsworth started it, and its casts mixed northeast Louisiana pickers and singers with well-known visitors: Ray Price, Jerry Lee Lewis, James Burton, Martha Carson, Merle Kilgore, Johnny Horton and Floyd Cramer all appeared. West Monroe's city hall and convention center now occupy the site, where the Northeast Louisiana Music Trail dedicated its fourteenth marker on November 17, 2023.

name: Po' Henry and Tookie marker
writeup: Henry Dorsey, a guitarist and singer born in 1928, and harmonica player Tookie Collom, born in 1937, both came from cotton sharecropping families. They began playing together in Rayville in 1986 and, as Po' Henry and Tookie, took the older acoustic Delta blues of northeast Louisiana, songs like "Trouble in Mind" and "Sittin' on Top of the World," to the Louisiana Folklife Festival, the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival and the Smithsonian's Festival of American Folklife in 1997. They received the Louisiana Governor's Arts Award for folk artist of the year in 2005. The Northeast Louisiana Music Trail unveiled this marker in downtown Rayville on June 4, 2022.

name: Choctaw-Apache Tribe of Ebarb Pow Wow Grounds
writeup: The Choctaw-Apache Tribe of Ebarb, recognized by Louisiana in 1978, is the state's second-largest tribe, with more than seven thousand citizens, half of them in Sabine Parish. It holds its powwows on its own tribal grounds near Zwolle, where permanent grounds were established in 2011. The tribe describes the annual Pow Wow as a celebration of culture, tradition and living Indigenous presence, with intertribal dancing, drum groups, Native artisans and shared food. The community traces its roots to eighteenth-century Spanish and French colonial settlements, including Los Adaes, and members are again studying their ancestral languages and practicing traditional social dances.
